q: In the stirrup spacing formula s = Av fyt d / Vs, what is fyt?
o: The yield strength of the stirrup steel
The yield strength of the main bars
n: fyt is the yield strength of the transverse (shear) reinforcement. Stirrups are often a lower grade than the main bars, so the two must not be mixed up.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is the minimum area of shear reinforcement Av,min where stirrups are required?
o: The larger of 0.062√f'c bw s/fyt and 0.35 bw s/fyt
Zero if the concrete carries the shear
n: The two terms make sure there is enough steel to carry the load when the first diagonal crack forms. The older code used bw s / (3fy), which is close to the 0.35 term.

q: How is the shear the stirrups must carry, Vs, found in design?
n: The nominal strength needed is Vu/φ. The concrete supplies Vc, and the stirrups must supply the rest.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what strength reduction factor φ applies to shear?
n: φ for shear is 0.75. The older code used 0.85 with different load factors; mixing the old φ with the new load factors is unsafe.

q: For a T-beam, which width is used as bw in the shear equations?
o: The total width of the floor
n: Shear is carried by the web, so bw is the web width. For a rectangular beam, bw is simply the beam width.

q: Under NSCP 2015, which construction is exempt from the minimum stirrup requirement?
n: Joists are closely spaced and share load, so the code exempts them, together with slabs, footings and very shallow beams.

q: Under NSCP 2015, below what overall depth is a beam exempt from the minimum stirrup requirement?
n: Beams with h ≤ 250 mm are exempt, because shallow members behave more like slabs.

q: Why are multi-leg stirrups used in wide or heavily loaded beams?
o: More legs cross each crack and hold more bars
n: A four-leg stirrup doubles Av at the same spacing and ties the interior bars too. Wide beams need legs spaced not far apart across the width.

q: What does shear reinforcement do in a concrete beam?
o: It carries tension across diagonal cracks
It carries the main bending tension
It carries the compression at the top
It stops shrinkage in the slab
n: Diagonal cracks form near the supports where shear is high. Stirrups crossing those cracks hold them together.

q: In shear design, what does s stand for?
n: s is measured along the beam from one stirrup to the next. Closer spacing means more steel crossing each crack.

q: What is Av for a two-leg 10 mm stirrup?
n: One 10 mm bar has an area of π(10)²/4 = 78.5 mm². A closed or U stirrup has two legs crossing the crack, so Av = 2 × 78.5 = 157 mm².
steps: Area of one 10 mm bar = π × 10² / 4 = 78.5 mm²

q: A beam needs Vs = 100 kN. It uses two-leg 10 mm stirrups (Av = 157 mm²), fyt = 275 MPa and d = 450 mm. What stirrup spacing does strength require?
n: s = Av fyt d / Vs = 157 × 275 × 450 / 100,000 = 194 mm. The code maximum (d/2 = 225 mm) must also be checked; here strength governs, so use about 190 mm.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is the maximum stirrup spacing where Vs is not more than 0.33√f'c bw d?
o: d/2, but not more than 600 mm
d/4, but not more than 300 mm
d, but not more than 1,000 mm
n: Every 45° crack must be crossed by at least one stirrup, so spacing is limited to d/2 (600 mm maximum). When Vs is high the limit halves to d/4 (300 mm maximum).

q: What is the effective depth d of a beam?
o: The total depth of the beam
Compression face to the centroid of tension steel
n: d is less than the overall height h by the cover, the stirrup and half the bar size. For a single layer, d ≈ h − 60 to 70 mm.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is the maximum Vs a beam section may be designed for?
o: Any amount, if enough stirrups are provided
n: Beyond Vs = 0.66√f'c bw d, the concrete struts between cracks would crush no matter how many stirrups are added, so the section must be enlarged.

q: Under NSCP 2015, when is a T-beam exempt from the minimum stirrup requirement?
o: When h ≤ the larger of 2.5hf and bw/2
n: Very shallow T-beams, whose depth is small compared with the flange or web, act more like thickened slabs, so the minimum stirrups are waived.

q: Under NSCP 2015, where must minimum stirrups be provided in ordinary beams?
o: Wherever the factored shear Vu exceeds 0.5φVc
Nowhere, if the concrete is strong
n: Even when concrete alone could carry the shear, a minimum amount of stirrups is required once Vu > 0.5φVc, to give ductility if a diagonal crack opens.

q: Why are closed stirrups used when a beam carries torsion?
o: Torsion cracks spiral around all four faces
They are easier to bend on site
n: Torsional shear flows around the perimeter. Open U-stirrups cannot carry it across the top, so closed stirrups with 135° hooks are required.

q: What characterizes a shear (diagonal tension) failure in a concrete beam?
o: Vertical cracks at midspan that widen slowly
Crushing at the top of midspan
An inclined crack near the support that opens suddenly
n: Diagonal tension cracks run at about 45° near the supports, where shear is highest. Without enough stirrups they can open suddenly and split the beam.

q: In shear design, what is Av?
o: The area of the main bars
The area of the beam web
The area of one stirrup leg
The area of all stirrup legs within spacing s
n: Av counts every leg that crosses the crack. A two-leg stirrup of 10 mm bar gives Av = 157 mm².

q: A beam has φVc = 120 kN. Above what factored shear Vu are stirrups required?
n: Minimum stirrups are required where Vu > 0.5φVc = 0.5 × 120 = 60 kN. Above φVc (120 kN), stirrups must also be designed for strength.

q: What is the nominal shear strength Vn of a reinforced concrete beam?
n: The concrete and the stirrups share the shear. The design check is φVn = φ(Vc + Vs) ≥ Vu.

q: A beam has f'c = 21 MPa, bw = 300 mm and d = 500 mm. Using the simplified formula Vc = 0.17√f'c bw d, what is Vc?
n: Vc = 0.17 × √21 × 300 × 500 = 0.17 × 4.58 × 150,000 = 116,900 N ≈ 117 kN. The older form (1/6)√f'c bw d gives almost the same value.

q: What is Vc in shear design?
o: The shear carried by the stirrups
The shear at the column face
The shear strength contributed by the concrete
n: Vc comes from the uncracked compression zone, aggregate interlock across cracks and dowel action of the main bars.

q: Which of these is exempt from the minimum stirrup requirement under NSCP 2015?
n: Slabs and footings spread shear over a wide width and are exempt from minimum stirrups. They are still checked for one-way and two-way (punching) shear.

q: At what section is the design shear usually taken for a beam loaded on top and supported from below?
o: At the center of the support
At a distance d from the support face
At the free end of the beam
n: Loads within d of the support go straight into it by arching, so sections closer than d may be designed for the shear at d.

q: What is a U-stirrup?
o: An open stirrup bent into a U
n: U-stirrups are open at the top and hooked around top bars. They are easy to place but cannot resist torsion; closed stirrups are needed then.

q: Why is shear failure more dangerous than flexural failure?
o: It is always slow and visible
It is brittle and gives little warning
n: Flexural failure of an under-reinforced beam gives large deflection first. Shear failure can split a beam suddenly, so shear design uses a lower φ and required minimum stirrups.
